title: Free-response workshop: Implicit differentiation and related rates
author: bc-workshop-author
directions: Work each question in 15 minutes, the exam's pace, writing answers in the space under each part. No calculator is allowed. Show supporting work, justify requested conclusions, and give exact answers. Then score your work with the answer key's rubric and record raw points.

figures.alt: A solid circular cylinder lying on its side. The radius r is marked from the center of the right end to its rim, and the length L is marked by a dimension line below the cylinder. Arrows at both ends point outward, under a note that reads: length grows; volume stays the same.
figures.caption: The clay coil at one instant.

figures.alt: Part of the curve x^2 + y^2 + xy^2 = 9 on axes with x from −1 to 4 and y from −5 to 5. The curve comes down steeply from the upper left, passes through (0, 3) and the marked point (1, 2), crosses the x-axis at x = 3, and continues below the x-axis as the mirror image of the upper half, through (0, −3). An open circle at the origin is labeled B.
figures.caption: Part of the robot's route. B is the beacon at the origin.

parts.directions: Show supporting work and justify requested conclusions. Give exact answers. No calculator is allowed.

items.prompt: Consider the curve given by x^2 − 2xy + y^3 = 4.

parts.label: a

rubric.criterion: Differentiates implicitly, with the product-rule terms −2y − 2x(dy/dx) from −2xy and the chain-rule term 3y^2(dy/dx) from y^3.

Collects the dy/dx terms and solves to reach the given expression; an equivalent arrangement such as (2x − 2y)/(2x − 3y^2) earns the point when the algebra is shown. A response that starts from the given answer earns neither point.

steps: Differentiate each term with respect to x: d/dx(x^2) = 2x; d/dx(−2xy) = −2y − 2x(dy/dx) by the product rule; d/dx(y^3) = 3y^2(dy/dx) by the chain rule; d/dx(4) = 0.
Keep the dy/dx terms on one side: (3y^2 − 2x)(dy/dx) = 2y − 2x.
Divide by 3y^2 − 2x and factor 2 from the numerator: dy/dx = 2(y − x)/(3y^2 − 2x).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write an equation for the line tangent to the curve at the point (3, 1). Use the tangent line to approximate the y-coordinate of the point on the curve near (3, 1) whose x-coordinate is 2.7.

rubric.criterion: Finds the slope 4/3 at (3, 1) and writes the tangent line y = 1 + (4/3)(x − 3), or an equivalent form.
Approximates the y-coordinate as 0.6, or the value given by the response's own tangent line at x = 2.7.

parts.answer: y = 1 + (4/3)(x − 3); at x = 2.7 the approximation is y ≈ 1 + (4/3)(−0.3) = 0.6.
steps: First confirm the point is on the curve: 9 − 6 + 1 = 4.
Tangent line: y = 1 + (4/3)(x − 3).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the value of d^2y/dx^2 at the point (3, 1). Given that d^2y/dx^2 has this same sign at every point of the curve between (3, 1) and the point in part (b), is the approximation in part (b) an overestimate or an underestimate? Give a reason for your answer.

rubric.criterion: Differentiates a second time correctly: either the quotient rule applied to 2(y − x)/(3y^2 − 2x) with dy/dx terms kept, or implicit differentiation of 2x − 2y − 2x(dy/dx) + 3y^2(dy/dx) = 0 that produces both 6y(dy/dx)^2 and (3y^2 − 2x)(d^2y/dx^2).
Substitutes x = 3, y = 1 and dy/dx = 4/3 to obtain d^2y/dx^2 = 22/9.
Concludes underestimate because d^2y/dx^2 > 0, so the curve is concave up there and lies above its tangent line. The conclusion must agree with the sign the response found.

parts.answer: d^2y/dx^2 = 22/9 at (3, 1). The approximation 0.6 is an underestimate: d^2y/dx^2 > 0 between the two points, so the curve is concave up there and lies above its tangent line.
steps: Differentiate 2x − 2y − 2x(dy/dx) + 3y^2(dy/dx) = 0 with respect to x: 2 − 2(dy/dx) − 2(dy/dx) − 2x(d^2y/dx^2) + 6y(dy/dx)^2 + 3y^2(d^2y/dx^2) = 0.
Solve: (3y^2 − 2x)(d^2y/dx^2) = 4(dy/dx) − 2 − 6y(dy/dx)^2.
Alternatively, the quotient rule gives d^2y/dx^2 = [2((dy/dx) − 1)(3y^2 − 2x) − 2(y − x)(6y(dy/dx) − 2)]/(3y^2 − 2x)^2 = [2(1/3)(−3) − 2(−2)(6)]/9 = 22/9.
A curve that is concave up on an interval lies above each of its tangent lines there, so the estimate is too small. (The curve's actual y-value at x = 2.7 is about 0.663, which agrees.)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find all points on the curve at which the line tangent to the curve is horizontal.

rubric.criterion: Sets the numerator of dy/dx equal to 0 (y = x) and substitutes into the equation of the curve to obtain x^3 − x^2 − 4 = 0, or an equivalent cubic.
Solves to find only (2, 2), with a reason that no other real solution exists (for example, x^2 + x + 2 has negative discriminant), and confirms the denominator 3y^2 − 2x = 8 is not 0 there.

steps: A horizontal tangent needs dy/dx = 0: the numerator 2(y − x) = 0 and the denominator 3y^2 − 2x ≠ 0.
y = x on the curve gives x^2 − 2x^2 + x^3 = 4, that is, x^3 − x^2 − 4 = 0.
x = 2 is a root, and x^3 − x^2 − 4 = (x − 2)(x^2 + x + 2). The quadratic has discriminant 1 − 8 = −7 < 0, so it has no real roots.
At (2, 2): 4 − 8 + 8 = 4, so the point is on the curve, and 3y^2 − 2x = 12 − 4 = 8 ≠ 0.

items.prompt: A potter rolls a lump of clay into a long coil. The coil stays a solid circular cylinder with radius r centimeters and length L centimeters, as shown in the figure, and its volume stays 72π cubic centimeters while she rolls. The length increases at a constant rate of 3 centimeters per second. The volume of the coil is V = πr^2L, and the area of its curved surface, not counting the two ends, is S = 2πrL.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the rate at which the radius of the coil is changing at the instant when r = 2 centimeters. Indicate units of measure.

rubric.criterion: Finds L = 18 cm at that instant from πr^2L = 72π.

Differentiates the volume relation with respect to t, using the product rule and dV/dt = 0: 0 = π(2rL(dr/dt) + r^2(dL/dt)). Accepts differentiating r^2L = 72, or L = 72/r^2, or r = √(72/L), when done correctly.
Obtains dr/dt = −1/6 cm/s, or states that the radius is decreasing at 1/6 centimeter per second, with units.

parts.answer: dr/dt = −1/6 cm/s: the radius is decreasing at 1/6 centimeter per second.
steps: At r = 2: π(4)L = 72π, so L = 18 cm.
The volume is constant, so differentiate πr^2L = 72π with respect to t: 2rL(dr/dt) + r^2(dL/dt) = 0.
Substitute r = 2, L = 18 and dL/dt = 3: 72(dr/dt) + 12 = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the rate at which S, the area of the curved surface, is changing at the instant when r = 2 centimeters. Is S increasing or decreasing at that instant?

rubric.criterion: Differentiates S = 2πrL with the product rule: dS/dt = 2π((dr/dt)L + r(dL/dt)), or uses S = 144π/r with the chain rule.
Obtains dS/dt = 6π cm^2/s and concludes that S is increasing; accepts a value consistent with the response's dr/dt from part (a).

parts.answer: dS/dt = 6π cm^2/s, so the curved surface area is increasing at that instant.
steps: dS/dt = 2π((dr/dt)L + r(dL/dt)).
The rate is positive, so S is increasing.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Show that S is increasing at every instant while the potter rolls the coil.

rubric.criterion: Expresses dS/dt in terms of r alone, dS/dt = 3πr, by using dr/dt = −3r/(2L) from the volume relation; or writes S = 2V/r = 144π/r together with dr/dt < 0.
Concludes dS/dt > 0 at every instant with the reason: r > 0, so 3πr > 0; or 144π/r increases as r decreases, and r is always decreasing. Checking one instant does not earn this point.

parts.answer: At every instant dS/dt = 3πr > 0, so S is always increasing. (Equivalently, S = 144π/r and r is always decreasing.)
steps: From 2rL(dr/dt) + r^2(dL/dt) = 0 with dL/dt = 3: dr/dt = −3r/(2L) at every instant.
Then dS/dt = 2π((dr/dt)L + 3r) = 2π(−3r/2 + 3r) = 3πr.
The radius is always positive, so dS/dt = 3πr > 0 throughout.
Check against part (b): r = 2 gives 6π.
Alternative: L = 72/r^2, so S = 2πr(72/r^2) = 144π/r. Since dr/dt = −3r/(2L) < 0, r decreases, and 144π/r increases as r decreases.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Use the line tangent to the graph of r as a function of t, at the instant when r = 2 centimeters, to estimate the radius 0.6 second later. Is this estimate an overestimate or an underestimate? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Estimates the radius as 2 + (−1/6)(0.6) = 1.9 cm, or the value consistent with the response's dr/dt from part (a).

Concludes underestimate because d^2r/dt^2 > 0 (r is concave up as a function of t), so the graph of r lies above its tangent line. Needs a correct reason that d^2r/dt^2 is positive on the interval, not only at the instant.

parts.answer: r ≈ 1.9 cm. It is an underestimate: d^2r/dt^2 > 0 throughout, so the graph of r is concave up and lies above its tangent line.
steps: Tangent-line estimate: r ≈ 2 + (dr/dt)(0.6) = 2 − (1/6)(0.6) = 1.9 cm.
Measure time u in seconds from that instant. Then L = 18 + 3u, and r = √(72/L) = 6√2(18 + 3u)^(−1/2).
Alternatively, differentiate dr/dt = −3r/(2L): d^2r/dt^2 = −(3/2)(L(dr/dt) − 3r)/L^2, which is positive because dr/dt < 0. At the instant it equals 1/24 cm/s^2.
A function that is concave up lies above its tangent line, so 1.9 cm is too small. (The actual radius is √(72/19.8) ≈ 1.907 cm.)

items.prompt: A delivery robot drives on a warehouse floor. Part of its route follows the curve x^2 + y^2 + xy^2 = 9, where x and y are measured in meters; the figure shows part of this curve. A charging beacon B sits at the origin. At time t seconds the robot is at the point (x(t), y(t)) on the curve, where x(t) and y(t) are differentiable functions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find dy/dx in terms of x and y. Then find all points on the curve x^2 + y^2 + xy^2 = 9 at which the line tangent to the curve is vertical.

rubric.criterion: Finds dy/dx = −(2x + y^2)/(2y + 2xy), or an equivalent expression.
Sets the denominator 2y(1 + x) equal to 0 and rules out x = −1, which gives 1 = 9, so y = 0.
Finds both (3, 0) and (−3, 0) from x^2 = 9 and confirms that the numerator 2x + y^2 = ±6 is not 0 there.

parts.answer: dy/dx = −(2x + y^2)/(2y + 2xy). The tangent line is vertical at (3, 0) and (−3, 0).
steps: Differentiate: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) + y^2 + 2xy(dy/dx) = 0, so (2y + 2xy)(dy/dx) = −(2x + y^2).
A vertical tangent needs the denominator 2y(1 + x) = 0 with the numerator not 0.
If x = −1, the equation becomes 1 + y^2 − y^2 = 9, which is false, so the curve has no points with x = −1.
So y = 0, and then x^2 = 9: x = 3 or x = −3.
The numerator 2x + y^2 equals 6 at (3, 0) and −6 at (−3, 0), so neither is 0/0. Both tangents are vertical; (−3, 0) lies on a part of the curve outside the figure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The robot passes through the point (1, 2) at an instant when dx/dt = −0.4 meter per second. Find dy/dt at that instant. Indicate units of measure.

rubric.criterion: Relates the rates: (2x + y^2)(dx/dt) + (2y + 2xy)(dy/dt) = 0, or dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt) with dy/dx = −3/4 at (1, 2).
Obtains dy/dt = 0.3 m/s, with units.

steps: Differentiate the curve's equation with respect to t: (2x + y^2)(dx/dt) + (2y + 2xy)(dy/dt) = 0.
At (1, 2): 6(dx/dt) + 8(dy/dt) = 0, which is the same as dy/dt = (−3/4)(dx/dt).
With dx/dt = −0.4: 8(dy/dt) = 2.4, so dy/dt = 0.3 m/s.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: At the instant described in part (b), is the distance between the robot and the beacon increasing or decreasing? Find the rate at which this distance is changing.

rubric.criterion: Writes D^2 = x^2 + y^2 (or D = √(x^2 + y^2)) and differentiates with respect to t: 2D(dD/dt) = 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt). Accepts D^2 = 9 − xy^2 differentiated correctly.
Obtains dD/dt = 0.2/√5 = √5/25 m/s and concludes that the distance is increasing; accepts a result consistent with the response's dy/dt from part (b).

parts.answer: dD/dt = 0.2/√5 = √5/25 m/s (about 0.089 m/s). The distance is increasing.
steps: Let D be the distance from B to the robot: D^2 = x^2 + y^2, so D(dD/dt) = x(dx/dt) + y(dy/dt).
So dD/dt = 0.2/√5 = √5/25 m/s, which is positive: the robot is moving away from the beacon.
Check: on the curve D^2 = 9 − xy^2, and differentiating gives 2D(dD/dt) = −((dx/dt)y^2 + 2xy(dy/dt)) = −(−1.6 + 1.2) = 0.4, the same result.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: At another time the robot passes through the point (3, 0). Use the equation relating dx/dt and dy/dt to find dx/dt at that instant. Explain what this tells you about the robot's motion there, and explain why dy/dt cannot be found from the equation of the curve alone.

rubric.criterion: Substitutes (3, 0) into (2x + y^2)(dx/dt) + 2y(1 + x)(dy/dt) = 0 to get 6(dx/dt) = 0, so dx/dt = 0.

Explains both: at that instant the robot moves parallel to the y-axis, along the vertical tangent (or is momentarily at rest); and the coefficient of dy/dt is 0 there, so the equation holds for every value of dy/dt and does not determine it. Accepts noting that more information, such as the robot's speed, would be needed.

parts.answer: dx/dt = 0 at (3, 0). The robot is moving parallel to the y-axis there, along the vertical tangent, or is momentarily at rest. The term with dy/dt has coefficient 2y(1 + x) = 0, so the equation reads 6(dx/dt) = 0 for any dy/dt and cannot determine it.
steps: The related-rates equation is (2x + y^2)(dx/dt) + 2y(1 + x)(dy/dt) = 0.
With dx/dt = 0, the velocity has no horizontal component: the robot is moving parallel to the y-axis, the direction of the vertical tangent found in part (a), unless it is at rest.
Every value of dy/dt satisfies 6(0) + 0·(dy/dt) = 0, so the curve alone does not fix dy/dt. A further fact, such as the robot's speed, would.
This agrees with the geometry: on this part of the route 1 + x > 0, so x^2 = 9 − y^2(1 + x) ≤ 9 and x is at most 3. At (3, 0), x(t) has a maximum, so its derivative is 0.
